question: Serious concerns have been raised1 concerning the gaps that exist in the Commission’s implementing acts, which establish the technical features of the European digital identity wallet (eIDAS)2, regarding the protection of privacy and the personal data of EU citizens.

Despite the additional reassurances given by the European Parliament and the Council in the new eIDAS regulation, the current implementing acts do not fully reflect these requirements, leaving major gaps in user protection.

Specifically: - A clear mechanism for limiting the data that relying parties are allowed to ask for is lacking, exposing users to requests to hand over too much personal data and to excessive personal data collection; - Complaints and requests to have data deleted are not handled in the same way across EU countries, which limits the rights afforded under the GDPR3; - The regulatory provisions do not guarantee unlinkability4 and unobservability5, making surveillance of user transactions possible, in violation of the eIDAS regulation.
In view of this: 1.

How does the Commission plan to ensure full compliance with the requirements of the GDPR and the eIDAS regulation with regard to the protection of privacy and guaranteed unlinkability and unobservability?

What steps will it take to ensure the interoperability and cross-border harmonisation of processes for lodging complaints and requesting data deletion, so as to harmonise the rights of users across the EU?
How does it plan to ensure the deterrence of requests for too much personal data and the excessive collection of user data?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.1.2025) Compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation1 (GDPR) and the European Digital Identity Framework2 (eIDAs Regulation), including privacy, unlinkability and unobservability, is supervised by the relevant competent authorities.

To further strengthening privacy, the European Digital Identity Wallets (the wallets) will need to be certified as part of a conformity assessment evaluating whether the wallets apply privacy preserving techniques ensuring unobservability and unlinkability. The implementing acts setting out the certification regime and the main features of the wallets were published on 4 December 20243.

Harmonisation of processes for lodging complaints and requesting data deletion is not foreseen in the GDPR, so each Member State is responsible for establishing the detailed procedural arrangements regarding the handling of complaints. Nonetheless, the wallets should contain an automatic tool for reporting to the relevant data protection authorities.

In addition, the wallets shall enable the user to easily request the erasure of personal data from a relying party pursuant to the GDPR. Both the GDPR and the eIDAS Regulation already establish limitations to the processing of personal data by wallet relying parties. One of the key principles of the eIDAS Regulation is that the wallet users maintain complete control over their data.

Combined with the purpose limitation principle established in the GDPR, this limits the data that relying parties are allowed to request and process from the wallets. The Commission is fully committed to ensuring the highest level of data privacy and security for the implementation of the European digital identity wallets.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of

natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1-88, https://eurlex.europa.
